reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The only official adoption measure in this material comes from the Census Bureau. Its Business Trends and Outlook Survey covers religious organizations inside the broader Other services category, NAICS 81, and the latest figure is 15.0%, against a prior period of 13.7%. The question behind that number is narrow: in the last two weeks, did this business use AI. The survey first asked about AI in September 2023, and the Census Bureau suppresses figures where the sample does not support them. Because the category lumps religious organizations together with other service firms, the figure describes the sector's neighborhood rather than congregations alone.

On what the technology is actually used for, the clearest vendor account comes from Gloo, which describes itself as delivering values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, with AI positioned as a foundational capability across its platform to support mission effectiveness and preserve relational ministry. Gloo says developers building in its AI Studio work with production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models, and it offers API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows with dynamic model selection per request. Barna Group is described here as running the national studies, with its State of the Church work quantitatively tracking AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders. The Barna page excerpts themselves center on pastoral leadership, the State of Pastors report, and why young adults attend church, so they do not supply specific AI adoption numbers.

Money and vendor concentration point in a few directions. Gloo is described as used by thousands of US churches and as surveying faith leaders while building AI tooling for ministry, which makes it the sector's primary commercial platform in this material. AI and Faith operates as an interfaith nonprofit network that solicits tax-deductible donations and runs a monthly newsletter, so its role is convening rather than selling. Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life, which places academic money behind the ethics side rather than deployment.

The regulatory and ethical posture in these sources is voluntary and values-driven rather than compliance-driven. AI and Faith frames its work around five strategic pillars and argues that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom to guide AI development, noting that 85 percent of the world's population claims a religious affiliation and that these issues are deeply spiritual as well as moral. It describes its aim as injecting humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected both. Notre Dame's material adds a caution about labor: Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher who meets with AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper. Lily Abadal, a partner at Catholic school consultants Partners in Mission and a faculty fellow with a Notre Dame project called DELTA, Human Formation in the Age of AI, is quoted saying AI awareness has been evolving.

Two of the cited organizations are largely silent on AI in the excerpts available. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research is described as having a 45 year history of accurate research on churches and congregational life and as regularly surveying congregational trends and digital adoption, but the harvested page text states only that history and no AI findings. Pew Research Center's religion page excerpts cover religious hostilities across countries, Latter-day Saints demographics, views of Muslims, Catholic opinion on Pope Leo XIV, abortion, converts, and religious diversity, and none of that addresses AI use in congregations, even though Pew is described as periodically measuring how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest conclusion. The official measure puts AI use in this broad service category at 15.0%, so adoption is real but far from universal, and the sector's own research infrastructure, Barna, Gloo, Hartford, and Pew, is described as tracking the question without the excerpts here showing the results. The vendors selling into the space emphasize values alignment and relational ministry rather than cost reduction, and the ethics organizations emphasize humility, human formation, and the human cost of displacement. A congregation weighing a tool should expect little regulatory guidance and should look for the specific survey findings from Barna, Gloo, Hartford, or Pew before treating any adoption claim as settled.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The University of Notre Dame’s Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to address pressing ethical issues, including artificial intelligence and other technology ethics. The institute states that it engages stakeholders to examine real-world challenges and provide practical models for ethical technology design, development, and deployment. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher, reports that many AI industry workers speak casually about job displacement and the prospect of faster, cheaper work, with some hoping to move beyond work entirely toward family time and hobbies. Lily Abadal, a partner at Partners in Mission and professor at the University of South Florida, notes that awareness of AI has been evolving; she is also a faculty fellow with Notre Dame’s DELTA project on human formation in the age of AI.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group presents itself as a Christian research organization offering data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry. The page advertises a free webcast replay that examines six trends affecting pastoral leadership, drawing on findings from its report *The State of Pastors, Volume 2*. It also promotes a podcast in which pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discuss challenges and opportunities in church leadership. Additionally, Barna reports new data on the social motivators behind why young adults attend church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind, organised under five strategic pillars. It argues that these issues are at root deeply moral, and that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation they are also deeply spiritual, so the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide AI's development and use. The organisation says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around artificial intelligence and related technologies. It quotes a statement that its goal is to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, calling the project deeply humanistic and one that draws on faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions. The page also invites tax-deductible donations and signups to a monthly newsletter.
